request.prompt: Which humanoid robots have SDK access?

result.text:
As of October 2026, several humanoid robots offer developer SDKs, APIs, or ROS 2 interfaces that allow external developers to program robot behavior, control joints, integrate sensors, build AI applications, and experiment with locomotion and manipulation.

The important distinction is between public SDK access, commercial developer access, and restricted enterprise access.

Humanoid robots with developer SDK access

1. Public or relatively open developer access

Unitree G1

Public SDK

C++ and Python SDKs.

Low-level joint control and high-level motion interfaces.

ROS 2 integration.

Simulation and reinforcement-learning workflows.

Particularly suitable for AI and robotics development.

Documentation: Unitree developer portal · GitHub SDK

Unitree H1

Public SDK

C++ and Python interfaces.

Low-level motor and motion control.

ROS 2 / DDS integration.

Locomotion and reinforcement-learning development.

Official SDK documentation

Reachy 2

Open source

Python SDK.

ROS 2 Humble.

Open-source software and hardware.

Manipulation, perception and teleoperation.

Developer documentation

LimX Dynamics TRON1

Public developer repositories and low-level SDK resources.

C++ and Python development.

Simulation and reinforcement-learning tools.

ROS integration.

Developer ecosystem overview

2. Other robots with documented SDK or development interfaces

3. Commercial robots with more restricted developer access

These are worth investigating, but having a developer program or integration interface does not necessarily mean anyone can download a complete SDK.

Agility Digit – Commercial and enterprise integration.

Figure 02 – Primarily controlled through Figure's own software ecosystem.

Apptronik Apollo – Commercial development and integration.

Fourier GR-1 – Research and development configurations.

Tesla Optimus – No generally available public developer SDK established.

For these, I would request written confirmation of API availability, documentation, and hardware-level access before purchasing.

Which should you choose?

My shortlist would be:

Important: What does SDK access actually mean?

Before selecting a robot, I would verify that its SDK provides:

Joint-level control: Direct access to individual motors and actuators.

Whole-body control: Ability to control arms, legs, torso and balance together.

Sensor access: Cameras, depth sensors, IMUs, force/torque sensors.

Python/C++ APIs: Ability to develop custom applications.

ROS 2 support: Integration with external robotics software.

AI integration: Ability to deploy custom perception, LLM and VLA models.

Simulation: URDF/MJCF models and support for MuJoCo, Isaac Sim or Gazebo.

Commercial licensing: Permission to deploy your own software on purchased hardware.

My strongest recommendation is the Unitree G1 EDU. It offers a particularly interesting combination of physical hardware access, SDK availability, ROS 2 and AI research capabilities.

One question that would help narrow this down:

Are you looking for a humanoid robot that you can program with your own AI software (for example, connecting an LLM or VLA model and giving the robot completely custom behaviors), or do you primarily want low-level hardware and motor-control access?

sources.label: ROS2 Support in Humanoid Robots: A Developer's Guide (2026)

result.markdown:
As of October 2026, several humanoid robots offer developer SDKs, APIs, or ROS 2 interfaces that allow external developers to program robot behavior, control joints, integrate sensors, build AI applications, and experiment with locomotion and manipulation.

The important distinction is between public SDK access, commercial developer access, and restricted enterprise access.

## Humanoid robots with developer SDK access

### 1. Public or relatively open developer access

Unitree G1

Public SDK

- C++ and Python SDKs.
- Low-level joint control and high-level motion interfaces.
- ROS 2 integration.
- Simulation and reinforcement-learning workflows.
- Particularly suitable for AI and robotics development.

Documentation: [Unitree developer portal](https://support.unitree.com/home/en/developer/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) · [GitHub SDK](https://github.com/unitreerobotics?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

Unitree H1

Public SDK

- C++ and Python interfaces.
- Low-level motor and motion control.
- ROS 2 / DDS integration.
- Locomotion and reinforcement-learning development.

[Official SDK documentation](https://support.unitree.com/home/en/developer/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

Reachy 2

Open source

- Python SDK.
- ROS 2 Humble.
- Open-source software and hardware.
- Manipulation, perception and teleoperation.

[Developer documentation](https://cornerstoneofhope.mashreqdevelopments.com/?_=%2Freachy-2%2F%23aU4iOhb7bFvlafZww2vsQW5YOT4MojBa9mn3&utm_source=chatgpt.com)

LimX Dynamics TRON1

- Public developer repositories and low-level SDK resources.
- C++ and Python development.
- Simulation and reinforcement-learning tools.
- ROS integration.

[Developer ecosystem overview](https://botlandscape.com/topics/software.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

### 2. Other robots with documented SDK or development interfaces

| Robot | Developer access | Main interfaces |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unitree H2 | Public documentation | SDK, C++, ROS-related tools |
| Unitree R1 | Public documentation | SDK development guide |
| Unitree G1-D | Developer documentation | SDK |
| Unitree H1-2 | SDK / research tooling | C++, ROS 2 |
| CASBOT 2 | Public ROS 2 SDK | C++, Python, ROS 2 |
| PAL TALOS | ROS 2 development ecosystem | ROS 2, MoveIt 2 |
| Leju Kuavo | Open-source development resources | ROS, simulation, control |

Sources: [宇树科技 文档中心](https://support.unitree.com/home/en/developer/)[GitHub](https://github.com/CasbotRobotics/casbot2-ros2-sdk)[ROS2 Support in Humanoid Robots: A Developer's Guide (2026)](https://biorobot.ai/en/blog/ros2-support-guide-humanoid-robots)[Robot developer ecosystems, SDKs, and simulation](https://botlandscape.com/topics/software.html)

### 3. Commercial robots with more restricted developer access

These are worth investigating, but having a developer program or integration interface does not necessarily mean anyone can download a complete SDK.

- Agility Digit – Commercial and enterprise integration.
- Figure 02 – Primarily controlled through Figure's own software ecosystem.
- Apptronik Apollo – Commercial development and integration.
- Fourier GR-1 – Research and development configurations.
- Tesla Optimus – No generally available public developer SDK established.

For these, I would request written confirmation of API availability, documentation, and hardware-level access before purchasing.

## Which should you choose?

My shortlist would be:

| Development objective | Best candidates |
| --- | --- |
| Full robot programming | Unitree G1, H1 |
| Python and AI integration | Reachy 2, Unitree G1 |
| Low-level motor control | Unitree G1, H1 |
| ROS 2 development | Reachy 2, Unitree, TALOS |
| Reinforcement learning | Unitree G1, H1, LimX |
| Industrial deployment | Digit, Apollo |
| Open-source experimentation | Reachy 2, CASBOT 2 |

## Important: What does SDK access actually mean?

Before selecting a robot, I would verify that its SDK provides:

1. Joint-level control: Direct access to individual motors and actuators.
2. Whole-body control: Ability to control arms, legs, torso and balance together.
3. Sensor access: Cameras, depth sensors, IMUs, force/torque sensors.
4. Python/C++ APIs: Ability to develop custom applications.
5. ROS 2 support: Integration with external robotics software.
6. AI integration: Ability to deploy custom perception, LLM and VLA models.
7. Simulation: URDF/MJCF models and support for MuJoCo, Isaac Sim or Gazebo.
8. Commercial licensing: Permission to deploy your own software on purchased hardware.

My strongest recommendation is the Unitree G1 EDU. It offers a particularly interesting combination of physical hardware access, SDK availability, ROS 2 and AI research capabilities.

One question that would help narrow this down:

Are you looking for a humanoid robot that you can program with your own AI software (for example, connecting an LLM or VLA model and giving the robot completely custom behaviors), or do you primarily want low-level hardware and motor-control access?
